system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2198-03-05 22:21:00 to 2198-03-10 14:18:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis s/p gastric pacer was readmitted three days after prior discharge for intractable nausea and vomiting. She presented with over 20 episodes of non-bloody, brown emesis and was found to have hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and sinus tachycardia. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, potassium repletion, and antiemetics including ondansetron, prochlorperazine, and lorazepam. Her blood pressure was controlled with IV metoprolol and transitioned to oral lisinopril. Gastric emptying study and upper GI with small bowel follow-through were normal, suggesting her symptoms were not due to motility or structural issues. Chronic microcytic anemia was identified, and iron supplementation was started. Due to recurrent symptoms without organic cause, outpatient brain MRI and psychiatric evaluation were recommended. Her diet was advanced to full, and she remained vomiting-free for two days prior to discharge. She was discharged home on her home medications with the addition of nightly lorazepam for nausea and anxiety.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

REASON FOR EXAMINATION:  Vomiting.

PA and lateral upright chest radiographs were reviewed in comparison to ___.

The central venous line tip is at the level of mid low SVC.  Heart size is
normal.  Mediastinal position, contour and width are unremarkable.  Lungs are
essentially clear.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  What
appears to be a pacemaker to the stomach due to gastroparesis is unchanged in
appearance.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of acute cardiopulmonary process.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis, and
persistent nausea and vomiting.

TECHNIQUE:  Non-enhanced and contrast-enhanced CT images of the head were
obtained.  Intravenous contrast was administered.

COMPARISON:  CT of the head from ___ and sinus CT from ___.

FINDINGS:

There is an unchanged small lacune in the anterior limb of the right internal
capsule (series 3, image 11).
There is no evidence of intracranial masses, hemorrhage, edema, shift of
normally midline structures, or acute infarctions.  The ventricles and sulci
are normal in size and caliber.  No fractures or soft tissue abnormalities are
identified.  The paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells are clear and well
aerated.

IMPRESSION:
1.  There is no evidence of intracranial masses, hemorrhage, or infarction.
2.  Unchanged small lacune in the anterior limb of the right internal capsule.

diagnoses.long_title: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been vomiting nonstop since yesterday morning. I can’t keep anything down—water, food, nothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain, fever, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no pain or fever. Just this awful nausea and vomiting. I had a really stressful day yesterday, and it started right after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of gastroparesis and Type 1 diabetes, this could be another flare-up. We’ll keep you NPO for now and give IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Last time, they thought it was gastroparesis too, but the tests were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw your records. You had a normal gastric emptying study recently. But since you’re having the same symptoms, we’ll treat it supportively for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll wait until your nausea improves. We’re giving you Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan through your IV to help control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. My blood sugar’s probably high too—I couldn’t take my insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 312 on arrival. We gave you some insulin and will adjust your regimen. The diabetes team will help fine-tune it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about that. My sugars have been harder to control lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Also, your blood pressure is quite high—172 over 112. That’s likely from the stress and not taking your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It always spikes in the hospital. I usually take lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV hydralazine to bring it down safely. Once you can take pills, we’ll restart your lisinopril and may add another medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but maybe a little less. I haven’t vomited since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep the anti-nausea meds going. Your labs show ketones in your urine, so your sugars are still a bit high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sign your body’s using fat for energy because it can’t use glucose well. We’re adjusting your insulin to fix that. Your Lantus dose will go up from 28 to 31 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Will I need to change my sliding scale too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the diabetes team is updating it to be more aggressive. We’ll give you the new instructions at discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a CT scan of your head. Since you can’t have an MRI because of your gastric pacer, this will help rule out any brain-related causes for the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right—I forgot about that. The MRI was planned last time, but my doctor said the pacer makes it unsafe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The CT with contrast will be a good alternative. It’s quick and should give us the answers we need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the CT scan showed no masses, bleeding, or stroke. Just a small old lacune, unchanged from before. So nothing in your brain is causing the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s probably my gastroparesis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. Even though your last motility test was normal, symptoms can still flare. We’ll keep treating it as such.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try sipping water today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, let’s try small sips. If you keep it down for a few hours, we’ll advance to ice chips, then clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great—no vomiting, and you tolerated the clear liquids. We’re going to try a soft diet this evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just take it slow. We’ll still keep the anti-nausea meds on board for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning! You made it through the night without vomiting. Your blood sugar is also improving—staying in the 150s with the new insulin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. What about my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still a bit high, so we’ve added oral metoprolol twice daily. We’re also increasing your lisinopril to 20 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken metoprolol before. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can lower your heart rate and blood pressure. We’ll monitor it. Some people feel tired at first, but it usually settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well—we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What meds will I be going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual meds. Lantus is now 31 units at night. Lisinopril is 20 mg daily, and you’ll start metoprolol 50 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have Zofran and Compazine tablets as needed. Plus, a new Compazine suppository—use it if pills don’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night went well—no nausea, good sleep. We’ll aim for discharge this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I see my endocrinologist soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your PCP and endocrinologist within a week. They’ll review your insulin changes and monitor your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set—you’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the new meds as directed, advance your diet slowly, and call if nausea returns or your sugars go out of control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll schedule those follow-ups today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really good. No nausea, ate breakfast without any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve made excellent progress. Stay hydrated, keep monitoring your sugars, and don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis was admitted for recurrent intractable nausea and vomiting, unable to tolerate oral intake. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and antiemetics including ondansetron, prochlorperazine, and lorazepam. Her blood glucose was elevated with ketonuria, prompting an increase in her Lantus dose from 28 to 31 units and adjustment of her sliding scale insulin. Hypertension, likely exacerbated by acute illness, was treated with IV hydralazine and transitioned to oral lisinopril 20 mg daily and metoprolol 50 mg twice daily. A CT head with contrast showed no central cause for her symptoms. Her nausea resolved, diet was advanced successfully, and she remained stable. She was discharged home with medication changes and instructions to follow up with her primary care provider and endocrinologist.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
